Residential Demolition in Kennewick, From Shed Teardowns to Whole Structures

Demolition around Kennewick is mostly the small-and-medium kind, and it tracks the age of the housing stock. Seventy-year-old neighborhoods generate a steady flow of teardown work: detached garages leaning past saving, additions from the 1970s coming off ahead of remodels, mobile homes clearing lots for stick-built replacement, in-ground pools nobody swims in, and — the quiet volume leader — concrete removal, as decades-old driveways, patios, and walkways come out ahead of new flatwork.

Demolition in Kennewick: what to know

The parts people underestimate are the paperwork and the disposal. Demolition of structures in Kennewick requires a permit, and buildings from before the mid-1980s trigger Washington's asbestos survey requirement — a certified inspection before demolition legally proceeds, because materials of that era (floor tile, siding, popcorn ceiling, duct wrap) routinely contain it. Disposal is tonnage economics: a small garage becomes many tons of debris, and how efficiently a contractor sorts (clean concrete recycles cheap; mixed debris pays full landfill rates) shows up directly in the bid.

We can connect you with demolition contractors covering the Tri-Cities for structures, pools, interior strip-outs, and concrete — permits, surveys, and haul-off handled.

Common demolition situations in Kennewick

Pre-1985 structures and the asbestos gate

The rule that surprises owners: before demolishing (and often before renovating) older structures, Washington requires an asbestos survey by a certified inspector, and any found material gets professionally abated first. Skipping it risks serious fines and contaminated debris nobody will accept. Legitimate contractors put the survey first in the timeline, not the fine print.

Pool fills that fail future use

Old pools come out two ways: partial demolition (walls broken down, drain holes punched, engineered fill) or full removal. Partial is cheaper but must be done right — a pool filled with unsorted debris and loose dirt becomes a sinkhole and a disclosure problem at sale. The compaction and documentation are the product.

Attached demolition that must respect the survivor

Taking down an addition, carport, or attached garage while preserving the house takes surgical sequencing — utility disconnects verified, shared framing separated by hand, weather-tight closure of the exposed wall. It's the demolition equivalent of dentistry, and it's bid accordingly.

How it works

  1. 1

    Scope, survey, and permits

    Site visit, asbestos survey where age triggers it, utility disconnect coordination (power, gas, water capped at the right points), and the city demolition permit. This front-end takes longer than the demolition.

  2. 2

    Abatement if needed

    Any identified asbestos-containing material comes out first via certified abatement — a separate regulated trade with its own documentation you keep forever.

  3. 3

    The takedown

    Machine demolition for detached structures (an excavator makes short work of a garage), hand-and-machine hybrid for attached work, sawing and breaking for concrete. Dust control matters in this wind — expect water spray on dry days.

  4. 4

    Sort, haul, and finish grade

    Concrete and metal sorted for recycling, remaining debris hauled and weighed, the site graded clean. The closing paperwork — disposal receipts, permit sign-off — is what future buyers and lenders will want to see.

What demolition costs in Kennewick

Demolition pricing in the Tri-Cities scales with volume, material, and access: sheds and small garages sit at the low end, mobile home removal mid-range, whole-house demolition the major line item — with disposal tonnage often a third or more of any bid. Asbestos survey costs are modest; abatement, when required, is its own budget that varies enormously with findings. Concrete removal prices per square foot by thickness, cheaper when a recycler takes clean loads. The bundling economics run strong: demolition plus excavation plus new-construction site prep from one mobilization beats three separate contractor visits.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a permit to tear down a shed or garage in Kennewick?

Structures beyond trivial size require a demolition permit through the city — and the permit process is what catches utility disconnects and survey requirements that protect you. Small prefab sheds under permit thresholds can typically come down freely; when in doubt, one phone call to the building department settles it.

How likely is asbestos in my old Kennewick building?

For pre-1980 construction, likely enough that the survey exists: vinyl floor tile and mastic, cement-asbestos siding, popcorn texture, and HVAC insulation are the frequent finds locally. A survey costing a few hundred dollars either clears the project or catches a health hazard before machines make it airborne — both outcomes are wins.

What does it cost to remove an old driveway?

Concrete removal prices by square footage and thickness — a typical two-car driveway is a routine half-day-to-day job with disposal the swing factor. Reinforced or extra-thick slabs take more breaking time. Booked together with the replacement pour, removal usually prices better than as a standalone.

Can a pool be filled in instead of dug out?

Yes — partial demolition with engineered fill is the standard budget path: break down the top walls, perforate the bottom for drainage, fill with compacted structural material, cap with topsoil. Done with compaction documentation it's a legitimate permanent solution; done carelessly it's a slow-motion sinkhole. Full removal costs more and returns the ground to unrestricted use.

How long does a residential demolition take?

The physical takedown is the fast part — a detached garage falls in a morning, a house in a day or two. The calendar is consumed by front-end steps: surveys, any abatement, utility disconnect scheduling, and permits, which together typically run a few weeks. Plan the project around the paperwork, not the excavator.
